# Brief: replace the new-starter onboarding process with something that works

We hired forty-one people last year and we will hire more this year. The
onboarding process was designed when we hired six a year and it has not been
revisited since. It is now the single most common complaint in the
three-month new-starter survey, and the complaints are specific and fair.

## What happens today

A new starter is sent a welcome email with eleven attachments. They fill in four
forms, three of which ask for the same information. Their equipment is ordered
on their first day rather than before it, so they spend the first week on a
loaner. Access to systems is requested individually by their manager, by email,
to five different people, and typically completes some time in week two. There
is a half-day induction on the first Monday of each month, which means a person
who starts on the third of the month waits four weeks for it.

None of the individual pieces are unreasonable. The problem is that there are
nineteen of them, they are owned by six different people, and nobody owns the
whole.

## What I want

Someone to own the whole, and a process that works from the offer acceptance
rather than from the start date. Most of what goes wrong is a thing that could
have been done in the two weeks before the person arrived and was not, because
nothing triggers until day one.

Specifically:

- One intake. The information a new starter provides is provided once, and
  everything downstream draws on it. Where a regulator requires a specific form,
  the form is generated from the intake rather than filled in again.
- Equipment ordered on acceptance, configured before arrival, on the desk on day
  one. This is the single change that would move the survey most.
- Access provisioned from the role, not from the manager's memory. A new
  engineer gets what an engineer gets. Exceptions are exceptions and are
  requested explicitly.
- Induction on demand rather than monthly. Most of it is content that does not
  need to be delivered live; the part that does can run weekly with two people
  in the room.
- A named buddy, assigned before arrival, with a short written description of
  what the buddy is actually expected to do. "Be available" produces nothing.

## Constraints

- We are not buying an onboarding platform. We have three systems that between
  them hold everything needed and the problem is coordination, not capability.
- Whatever you design has to work for the fully remote starters, who are about a
  third of hires and who currently have a worse experience than the office ones
  in every respect.
- The regulated roles have requirements that cannot be streamlined away. Find
  out exactly what those are from compliance rather than assuming; my
  understanding is that it is less than people think.

## Deliverables

- The redesigned process, described as a timeline from offer acceptance to day
  thirty, with an owner named for every step.
- The intake form, and a list of what each downstream system needs from it.
- A pilot with the next five starters, measured against the current experience
  using the same survey questions so the comparison is real.
- A short written statement of who owns this ongoing. If the answer at the end
  of the project is "nobody", it will be back where it started within a year.

## Where the resistance will come from

Not from the six owners. They all dislike the current arrangement and none of
them chose it.

It will come from the fact that the redesign makes visible how long things
actually take. Access provisioning is quoted as two days and takes nine; when
that is on a timeline with a name against it, the person named will want to
argue about the number rather than about the process. Have the data before you
have that conversation, and frame it as the process being wrong rather than the
person being slow, which is true.

## Timing

Six weeks to the design, then the pilot with the next five starters, then a
review. Do not try to fix everything before the pilot. A pilot that runs on
three of the five changes and measures them is worth more than a complete design
that has never met a real new starter.
